name: Peace Lily
description: The Peace Lily (Spathiphyllum species) is a popular indoor houseplant. Despite its name, it is not a true lily and does not cause the fatal kidney failure in cats associated with true lilies. However, it is still moderately toxic and can cause intense discomfort if chewed. The leaves and stems contain tiny, needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. When a cat bites the plant, these sharp crystals are released, physically piercing the delicate tissues of the mouth, tongue, and throat. This causes immediate, intense burning and pain, which usually stops the cat from eating more of the plant. A cat that bites a peace lily will often start drooling heavily, pawing at its mouth, and may have trouble swallowing. It might also vomit if it swallowed any plant matter. You can gently rinse your cat's mouth with water to help clear the crystals. Contact a veterinarian if the drooling continues or if throat swelling makes it hard for your cat to breathe or swallow.
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: insoluble calcium oxalate raphides throughout leaves, stems, and flowers
Mechanism: crystals penetrate the oral mucosa mechanically, causing burning, swelling, and inflammation
Symptoms: intense drooling, pawing at mouth, oral pain, difficulty swallowing, vomiting
No kidney failure risk — Peace Lily is NOT a true lily; the name is misleading but the toxicity is different and milder
Rinse the mouth with water; seek vet care if throat swelling impairs swallowing or breathing

symptoms.name: Intense burning, pain, irritation, erythema (redness), and pawing at the mouth
symptoms.notes: This immediate pain is caused by the needle-like insoluble calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) physically piercing the mucous membranes as the cat bites into the plant14. This intense, sudden pain usually limits the amount of the plant the cat actually consumes.

symptoms.name: Hypersalivation (excessive drooling) and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
symptoms.notes: This is a direct response to the oral trauma and tissue swelling (edema) in the tongue and pharynx46. Rinsing the cat's mouth out with water or offering a calcium-containing dairy product (like milk) can help bind the crystals and soothe the irritation.

symptoms.name: Vomiting, stomach upset, and occasionally diarrhea
symptoms.notes: If the cat manages to swallow the plant material, the crystals will continue to irritate the gastrointestinal tract, causing vomiting and diarrhea2. However, this irritation remains localized and does not cause systemic organ failure.

symptoms.name: Lethargy and anorexia (refusal to eat)
symptoms.notes: Because the cat's mouth and throat are inflamed and in pain, they will often refuse food and appear lethargic or depressed.

symptoms.name: Difficulty breathing (dyspnea)
symptoms.onset: Immediate to shortly after exposure, as swelling progresses.
symptoms.notes: While generally rare and usually easily treatable, if the edema (swelling) spreads to the laryngeal region (the throat/airway), it can obstruct the airway and cause potentially life-threatening respiratory distress.
